Estimation, inference, and sampling in plain language. Every graph is a simulation I ran (20,000 simulated studies per panel unless noted), except the tea-tasting table and the Simmons et al. bars, which come straight from your slides. The quiz is conceptual with no calculations, so focus on the "why".

1. p-values2. Multiplicity3. p-hacking4. Power5. Estimates & CIs6. Bayes factorsCheat sheet
The one-sentence map Estimation asks "what is the effect in my sample?" Inference asks "what does my sample tell me about the population?" A p-value, a confidence interval, and a Bayes factor are three different tools for the second question.

1. p-values

The idea in one picture

Imagine the treatment truly does nothing. If you ran the experiment over and over, your estimated effect would still wobble around zero just from sampling noise. That wobble is the null distribution. A p-value asks: if the null were true, how often would I get a result at least as extreme as the one I got?

A p-value IS
  • P(data this extreme or more | null is true)
  • A statement about the data under one assumed world (the null)
  • Fisher's use: p < .05 lets you reject the null, and that is all
A p-value is NOT
  • The probability the null is true (so p = .05 does not mean "5% chance the null is true")
  • The size or importance of an effect (significant does not mean clinically important)
  • Proof of no effect when p ≥ .05
  • The probability the result will replicate

The Harry Potter way to remember it

Harry gets a letter from Hogwarts. The p-value is like P(letter | not a wizard), which is tiny. But what Harry wants is P(wizard | letter). To get that you also need P(letter | wizard) and how common wizards are (the base rate). A p-value alone leaves both out. That is the core of "p-values don't tell you what you want to know."

What the distribution of p-values looks like

Memorize this Under the null: flat (uniform) histogram. Any p-value is equally likely, so p < .05 happens 5% of the time, p < .01 happens 1% of the time, and so on.
Under a true effect: skewed toward 0. The more power, the stronger the pile-up. The share of p-values below .05 is the power.

Also from the slides: a bigger sample gives a tighter null distribution, so a smaller effect is enough to reach p < .05. And "the p-value is an inferential statistic" because it is used to say something about a population-level hypothesis (the null), not just describe your sample.

Quick check: Is “p = .03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true” correct?

No. It is the probability of data this extreme given the null, not the probability of the null given the data. Getting the second one needs a prior (base rate) and the likelihood under the alternative.

Quick check: If every null hypothesis in a field were true, what would a histogram of all the p-values look like?

Flat. About 5% below .05 and about 1% below .01.

Quick check: Is p = .04 from a tiny study “the same evidence” as p = .04 from a huge study?

Not necessarily. Same p-value does not mean the same evidence or the same effect size (dirty-dozen misconception #5). A big study can hit p = .04 with a tiny effect; a small study needs a large one.

2. Multiplicity

Each test has a 5% false-positive chance when the null is true. Run many tests and the chances that at least one comes out significant add up:

P(at least one false positive) = 1 − (0.95)k

Intuition: buying one lottery ticket gives you a 5% chance; buying 20 gives you 64%. You did not get better at winning; you got more tickets.

Fixes: reduce the number of tests, correct for them (Bonferroni and relatives), and preregister which tests count. The slides tie this to overfitting: with enough tests you will eventually "explain" noise.

Quick check: “Does an estimation strategy get you out of this mess?” (a question on your slides)

Only partly. This is my reasoning rather than something the slides spell out. A 95% CI that excludes zero is equivalent to p < .05, so if you compute 20 CIs on null effects you will still expect about one that excludes zero. What estimation does help with is emphasis: it makes you report how big each effect is and how uncertain it is, so a lone “significant” result among many looks less impressive. You still need to report everything you tested.

3. p-hacking

p-hacking is making data-dependent choices until p < .05 shows up. Each choice is a hidden extra "ticket" (multiplicity in disguise), and only the lucky one gets reported.

FlavorWhat it looks likeWhy it inflates false positives
Optional stoppingCheck p after every few participants; stop as soon as p < .05; otherwise keep collectingEarly noise can dip below .05 at some point, and you get to stop at that moment. Many looks = many tickets.
Selective reporting of outcomesMeasure several DVs (or transformations), report the one that "worked"k outcomes = k tests, but you present it as one.
Flexible exclusions or subgroupsDrop outliers after seeing results, split by gender or native language post hoc, add or drop a conditionEvery possible exclusion rule or split is another test; the paths multiply.

Your slides also show a thesis example with annotations for optional stopping, an extra condition added later, and a post-hoc split, ending in a result with p = .07. Same ingredients, same problem.

How preregistration helps Before seeing data, write down the sample size or stopping rule, the primary outcome, exclusion rules, and the planned subgroups and analyses. Then your choices cannot depend on the data, so the 5% promise is honest again. Slide wording: pre-specify the data collection plan, then "analyze as much as you want" (as long as the confirmatory test was fixed in advance). Alternatives when you really need flexible stopping: sequential analysis (plan several looks and adjust alpha) or Bayesian approaches (collect until BF passes a set threshold).
Quick check: Why does optional stopping inflate false positives even though each individual p-value is computed correctly?

Because the p-value assumes a fixed sample size decided in advance. If you can stop whenever p dips below .05, the chance that some look crosses the line is far larger than 5%.

Quick check: Does preregistration forbid exploratory analyses?

No. It separates confirmatory tests (planned, honest p-values) from exploratory ones (labeled as such). You can still explore, but you must not present it as a planned test.

4. Statistical power

Power = the probability of getting p < .05 when the effect is real and has a specific size. It equals 1 − β, where β is the false-negative (Type II) rate.

Null is trueNull is false (real effect)
Reject nullType I error, false positive (α)Correct: power = 1 − β
Don't rejectCorrectType II error, false negative (β)

The three levers

LeverRaise it and power…Catch
Effect sizegoes up (the blue curve sits farther from the grey one)You do not control it; it is what you are trying to learn.
Sample size Ngoes up (curves get narrower)Costs time and money; the gains slow down.
Alphagoes up (cutoff moves toward the null)More false positives. In my example (d = .5, 50/group): α = .01 gives 45%, .05 gives 70%, .10 gives 80%.

The slides' "probing power intuitions" (my computed answers)

Assuming two-sided alpha = .05; t-tests use two independent equal groups with N total as given; correlations use the Fisher-z approximation.

ScenarioApprox. power
t-test, d = .5, N total = 24~22%
t-test, d = .8, N total = 36~65%
t-test, d = .3, N total = 120~37%
correlation, r = .5, N = 36~88%
correlation, r = .3, N = 80~78%

Takeaway: even "average psychology" effects (d around .5) with typical lab sample sizes have well under 80% power.

What underpowered studies do to the literature

  • Inflated published effects. Only the lucky overestimates cross p < .05 (with publication bias, the literature looks stronger than reality).
  • Misread null results. p > .05 in a low-powered study mostly means "I could not tell", not "no effect".
  • Bad replications. If you power a replication on an inflated published effect, your "well-powered" replication is actually underpowered (slide: post-hoc power suffers from bias).
  • Few real effects found, many false ones. Low power also lowers the share of significant results that are true.

Why pilots cannot estimate effect sizes

A pilot has few participants, so its effect-size estimate is extremely noisy (right panel above). Powering your main study on it can make you plan far too small or far too large. The slides say: don't do this. Better sources for the target effect size: a meta-analysis (still affected by publication bias), a prior finding you replicate (probably inflated, so adjust or be conservative), or the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI). Pilots are still fine for checking your procedure and measures work.

Quick check: You double your sample size. What happens to power, and what happens to alpha?

Power rises (null and alternative curves both narrow). Alpha stays at whatever you set it to, 5% by convention.

Quick check: A small study finds p = .02 with a huge effect. Why be cautious?

With low power, significant results are disproportionately lucky overestimates, so the observed effect is likely inflated relative to the true one.

Quick check: Why is “post-hoc power” not recommended?

It is computed from the observed effect, which is noisy and, if the study was significant under low power, inflated. It mostly restates the p-value rather than adding information. The slides prefer a priori power or sample-size justification (including SESOI and precision).

5. Estimates and confidence intervals

Effect size: Cohen's d

d = (mean1 − mean2) / SD

It expresses the difference between groups in "how many standard deviations apart," which makes studies with different scales comparable. Rough labels: .2 small, .5 medium, .8 large. At d = .5, the average treated person scores higher than about 69% of controls (slide table). Downsides: it depends on variability, and raw units (200 ms, .2 GPA points) can be more meaningful, so the slides suggest reporting both.

Why smaller studies are noisier

Repeat an experiment many times and the estimates form a sampling distribution. Its center is the true effect (on average), but its spread is the standard error: SEM = SD / √N. Small N means large SE, so any single small study can land far from the truth, in either direction. This is why a bigger sample "tightens" the distribution of estimates.

What a 95% confidence interval is

A 95% CI DOES tell you
  • The procedure captures the true value in about 95% of repeated studies
  • How precisely you estimated the effect (narrow = precise)
  • Which effect sizes are reasonably compatible with your data
  • If it excludes 0, that matches p < .05 (two-sided)
A 95% CI does NOT tell you
  • That there is a 95% probability the true value is in this interval (the truth is fixed; the interval is what varies)
  • That 95% of the data lie inside it
  • That 95% of future estimates will fall inside it
  • That values inside it are equally likely

Comparing an original study with its replications

Two cautions. First, the original CI is usually wide (small N), so many effect sizes are compatible with it. Second, "overlap" is not a magic test: judge the replication's own CI against zero and against the original estimate, and consider precision. From the slides, the "small telescopes" idea adds that if a replication shows an effect smaller than what the original study could even have detected (the effect size giving it 33% power), the original effect is probably not real at that size. A replication needs about 2.5 times the original N to test this well.

Quick check: Original study d = .6, 95% CI [.14, 1.07]. What does the CI say about the original?

The data are compatible with anything from a tiny effect to a very large one, and zero is just outside. It is a significant but imprecise estimate.

Quick check: Your slides gave you SEM but not SD. How do you get the SD for d?

SD = SEM × √N. You can also compute d from a reported t-statistic.

6. Bayes factors

A Bayes factor compares how well two hypotheses predict the data you observed:

BF10 = P(data | H1) / P(data | H0)

H1 is "there is a non-zero effect," H0 is "the effect is exactly zero." BF is evidence from the data alone; it does not include your prior odds. (Prior odds × BF = posterior odds.) Note that it still depends on the prior you place on the effect size under H1; the slides use a default JZS prior plus sensitivity analyses.

BF10Read it as
1The data do not favor either hypothesis.
3The data are 3 times more likely under H1 than under H0. Moderate evidence for H1.
10The data are 10 times more likely under H1. Strong evidence for H1 (the slides use |BF| > 10 as a stopping rule).
1/3 (= 0.33)The data are 3 times more likely under H0 than H1, so BF01 = 3. Moderate evidence for the null.

BF = 3 does not mean "H1 has a 75% chance of being true"; that conversion needs prior odds.

How it differs from a p-value

p-valueBayes factor
ComparesData against H0 onlyH1 against H0
Can show evidence for the null?No (a high p just means "not rejected")Yes (BF below 1, like 0.18)
OutputP(data this extreme | H0)Ratio of likelihoods, a graded measure of evidence
Needs a stated H1?Not in Fisher's versionYes (a prior on the effect size)
Stopping ruleMust fix N in advance (or adjust alpha)Can run sequentially until BF passes a threshold
Quick check: A study reports BF10 = 0.18. What can you conclude?

The data are about 5.5 times (1/0.18) more likely under the null than under H1, which is moderate evidence for no effect. A p-value could not have said this.

Quick check: Is BF = 3 the same as “75% probability H1 is true”?

No. BF is a likelihood ratio. To get a probability for H1 you must multiply by the prior odds.

One-line cheat sheet

TopicIf asked, say…
p-valueP(data this extreme or more | null true). Not P(null | data), not effect size, not proof of absence. Flat under the null; skewed to 0 under a true effect.
Multiplicityk tests at .05 give 1 − .95k chance of at least one false positive (about 10% for 2, 64% for 20). Fix: fewer tests, correction, preregistration.
p-hackingData-dependent choices (stopping, outcomes, exclusions, subgroups) = hidden extra tests. Preregister the plan to make the choices independent of the data.
PowerP(significant | real effect) = 1 − β. Depends on effect size, N, alpha. Low power: noisy, inflated significant results; null results uninformative. Do not power from pilots.
Estimates / CId = mean difference in SD units. Small N means large SE (SD/√N). 95% CI = a procedure that captures the truth 95% of the time. Compare original vs replication CIs on zero, on the original estimate, and on width.
Bayes factorBF10 = P(D|H1)/P(D|H0). 3 and 10 favor H1 (moderate, strong); 1/3 favors H0 by 3 to 1. Evidence from data alone, no prior odds. Can support the null, unlike p.

Numbers I simulated (p-value shares, optional-stopping rate, winner's-curse average, power values) will vary slightly from run to run; the patterns are what matter.
